title: Make your first blinking light
introduction: An LED is a tiny light that allows current to flow mainly in one direction. A resistor reduces the current. The UNO turns this light on and off automatically.
purpose: Build one visible circuit and learn to upload your very first program.
learn: Identify an LED, resistor and GND
Upload code and change a delay

parts.role: The small computer that follows your code
Limits current to protect the LED
Connects board pins and breadboard rows

extras: Computer with Arduino IDE 2 and an internet connection for initial installation.
USB Type-C data cable compatible with the listed UNO; confirm whether the board includes one.

wiring.note: Put the resistor legs in different connected rows.
Short lead / flat rim usually marks the cathode; verify untrimmed part.
Unplug before changing wires; no other supply is needed.

steps: Unplug the UNO. Place the LED long lead in row 10 and short lead in row 11 on the same side of the breadboard; keep the leads separate.
Connect the resistor from row 8 to row 10. A resistor has no positive or negative end.
Connect UNO D9 to row 8 and UNO GND to row 11. This creates one path: D9 → resistor → LED → GND.
Follow First-time setup below, then open and upload beginner-blinking-light.ino.
Watch for one second on, one second off. Change both 1000 values to 500, upload again, and compare.
expected: The external red LED is on for one second and off for one second, repeatedly.
Changing the delays to 500 makes the cycle twice as fast.
troubleshooting: No light
Unplug and check LED direction, D9, resistor and the exact numbered rows.
Always on
Check that the wire is on D9, not 5V.
Upload fails
Select Arduino Uno and the correct port; use a data cable and close other apps using that port.
Board becomes hot or USB disconnects
Unplug immediately. Check for a short between 5V and GND before reconnecting.
extension: Try 200 ms on and 1800 ms off. Predict the result before uploading.
notes: Unplug USB before building or changing any connection. Power only from computer USB for these small circuits.
On a typical breadboard, a–e in one numbered row are connected; f–j form a separate group. The center gap separates them. Different numbered rows are separate.
Do not put both LED leads or both resistor leads in the same connected row. Do not connect 5V directly to GND.
libraries: None — only Arduino AVR Boards core functions; tested with core 1.8.8
serial: Not needed unless a step asks for it
validation: Compile-checked with Arduino AVR Boards 1.8.8 (UNO). Physical hardware has not been bench-tested; check exact parts before connecting.
firstTime: Install Arduino IDE 2 from the official Arduino website on a computer. An IDE is the app used to send instructions to the board. No coding experience is needed.

Connect the UNO using a USB data cable. Open Boards Manager, search Arduino AVR Boards and install it. Choose Arduino Uno in the board selector, then select the port that appears when your board is connected.
Download the program below. Put the .ino file in a folder with the same name without .ino and open it. A sketch is simply an Arduino program.

Click Verify (check mark) to check the program, then Upload (right arrow) to send it to the board. Wait for the upload-complete message. If no port appears, try a known data cable; identify the board’s USB chip before installing its manufacturer driver.
setup() runs once when the board starts. loop() repeats. Lines beginning with // are explanations for you. HIGH switches an output on, LOW switches it off, and delay(1000) waits one second.

purpose: Discover how one simple output can communicate a message through timing. This is a classroom model, not an emergency signalling device.

Connect the short LED lead (cathode) to GND. Check the connection table.

purpose: Make a tabletop traffic-light model and understand a sequence of timed actions.
learn: Set a sequence and measure its timing

title: Read a knob on your computer
introduction: A potentiometer is a resistor with a movable contact called a wiper. Turning its knob changes the voltage at this contact. The UNO turns that voltage into a number and sends it to the computer.
purpose: See how a physical action becomes a number without connecting a screen or motor.

parts.role: The small computer that follows your code

parts.variant: 10 kΩ, three-terminal potentiometer; confirm terminal markings

parts.role: Connects board pins and breadboard rows

extras: Computer with Arduino IDE 2 and an internet connection for initial installation.
USB Type-C data cable compatible with the listed UNO; confirm whether the board includes one.

wiring.note: Use the terminal map for your exact part.
Do not confuse an end with the wiper.
Usually center terminal; verify before powering.
Unplug before changing wires; no other supply is needed.

steps: Identify the two end terminals and wiper using the part diagram or ask the seller to label them. Do not guess from an unfamiliar package.
Unplug USB. Insert the potentiometer so its terminals are in separate connected rows; use jumpers if needed.
Connect one end to UNO 5V and the other end to GND.
Connect only the wiper to A0. A0 reads a voltage; it does not power the knob.
Follow First-time setup and upload beginner-knob-reader.ino.
Open Tools → Serial Monitor in Arduino IDE and choose 9600 baud. This is a text window for messages from the board.
Turn the knob slowly from one end to the other and record minimum, middle and maximum values.
expected: Serial Monitor displays a new value about five times per second.
The number varies approximately from 0 to 1023; the middle is near 512. Small fluctuations are normal.
troubleshooting: Unreadable characters
Set Serial Monitor to 9600 baud to match Serial.begin(9600).
Number stays at 0 or 1023
Unplug and check the wiper wire to A0 and both supply ends.
Number rises in the opposite direction
This is normal. Unplug and swap the two end-terminal wires if desired; leave the wiper on A0.
Upload fails
Select Arduino Uno and the correct port; use a data cable and close other apps using that port.
Board becomes hot or USB disconnects
Unplug immediately. Check for a short between 5V and GND before reconnecting.
extension: Change delay(200) to delay(1000) and compare how often the number updates.
flow: Read A0 voltage as a number
notes: Unplug USB before building or changing any connection. Power only from computer USB for these small circuits.

title: Play a three-note tune

purpose: Make sound with a simple module and learn the difference between pitch and duration.

Unplug before changing wires; no other supply is needed.

Unplug USB and place the module so its terminals do not share connected breadboard rows.
Connect + to UNO 5V and − to GND.
Connect S to D3. Check all three labels against the diagram before plugging in USB.
Follow First-time setup and upload beginner-musical-buzzer.ino.
Listen at arm’s length: three rising notes, then silence, repeated. Unplug USB to stop.
Find tone(), delay() and noTone() in the code: they start a pitch, hold it, and stop it.

title: Build your first button-controlled LED
introduction: A microcontroller repeatedly reads an input and decides what to do with an output. This small circuit makes that loop visible: press a button and a red LED lights.
purpose: Learn the complete upload-and-test workflow before connecting more expensive sensors or actuators.
learn: Explain why inputs need a pull-up

parts.variant: Jumper set; select enough leads and correct connector types

extras: USB data cable and computer with Arduino IDE 2; cable must support data, not charging only.

wiring.note: Use opposite contact groups; D2 has an internal pull-up enabled in code.
LED flat side / short lead is usually cathode; verify if trimmed.
USB powers this low-current circuit.

steps: With power disconnected, identify the switch contact groups using continuity mode. The two legs on one side may already be joined.
Place the switch across the breadboard center gap. Connect D2 through the switch to GND.
Connect D9 through the 330 Ω resistor to the LED anode, and the cathode to GND.
In Arduino IDE select Arduino AVR Boards → Arduino Uno and the correct serial port. Open the downloaded sketch and upload.
Press and release the button repeatedly. The code accepts a new state only after it stays stable for 30 ms.
expected: Released: LED off. Pressed: LED on.
At 5 V with a roughly 2 V red LED, 330 Ω gives about 9 mA.
troubleshooting: LED never lights
Check LED polarity, resistor connection and selected board/port.
LED always on
Check switch contact grouping and accidental GND connection to D2.
extension: Modify the sketch to toggle the LED on each press. Detect a stable HIGH-to-LOW transition so holding the button does not toggle repeatedly.
notes: Disconnect USB before moving wires. A bare LED must have its series resistor.
validation: Compile-checked with Arduino AVR Boards 1.8.8 (UNO). Physical hardware and network operation have not been bench-tested; verify your exact modules.

title: Build an adjustable LED dimmer
introduction: A potentiometer creates a variable voltage. The UNO reads that voltage and uses pulse-width modulation to change the LED’s average brightness.
purpose: Connect an analog input to a controllable output, then observe how digital values describe physical settings.
learn: Distinguish PWM from a true variable DC output

parts.variant: Jumper set; select enough leads and correct connector types

extras: USB data cable and computer with Arduino IDE 2; cable must support data, not charging only.

wiring.note: The opposite end goes to GND.
Swapping the ends reverses knob direction.
The wiper is usually the center terminal; verify.
D9 supports PWM on UNO R3.
All grounds share a common reference.

steps: Identify the wiper terminal and end terminals with a meter.
Wire the potentiometer between 5 V and GND, with its wiper connected to A0.
Wire the LED and resistor to D9 as shown.
Select Arduino Uno, upload the sketch, and open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud.
Turn the knob slowly and compare the ADC/PWM values with the visible brightness.
expected: ADC moves approximately from 0 to 1023; PWM moves from 0 to 255.
At the minimum setting the LED is off; at maximum it is brightest.
troubleshooting: Reading stays at one end
Check the wiper wire and breadboard row placement.
Brightness does not change
Use D9, not a non-PWM pin; inspect the LED path.
extension: Limit the output to PWM 180 and explain why brightness perception does not increase linearly with the number.
notes: Never connect the potentiometer to a voltage above the UNO ADC supply.
validation: Compile-checked with Arduino AVR Boards 1.8.8 (UNO). Physical hardware and network operation have not been bench-tested; verify your exact modules.

title: Build an automatic night light
introduction: A photoresistor module senses relative brightness. Two thresholds turn an LED on in darkness and off in brighter conditions, avoiding flicker around a single switching point.
purpose: Introduce calibration and hysteresis using an accessible light-control project.
learn: Handle modules with reversed output direction

parts.variant: Analog photoresistor module with S/AO output
Jumper set; select enough leads and correct connector types

extras: USB data cable and computer with Arduino IDE 2; cable must support data, not charging only.

wiring.note: Use the module labels, not the physical pin order.
Common ground.
Use analog output, not DO if your board has both.
Place the LED so it does not shine into the sensor.
Low-current demonstration only.

steps: Wire the module and LED with USB disconnected.
Upload the sketch and open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. The initial 200/800 values are examples only.
Cover the sensor and record its raw value; illuminate it normally and record the bright value.
Replace DARK_READING and BRIGHT_READING with your measurements, then upload again. The code supports either slope direction.
Shade the sensor gradually. It should switch on below 30% relative light and remain on until light exceeds 45%.
expected: The LED switches at two different levels instead of rapidly flickering.
The percentage is a calibrated relative scale, not a lux measurement.
troubleshooting: Switches in reverse
Measure and correctly label dark/bright calibration values.
Oscillates after switching on
Move the LED away from the sensor or shield the sensor from its own lamp.
Calibration error
Use conditions giving at least 50 counts of separation.
extension: Record the raw reading at several locations and compare repeatability. Replace the LED with a properly driven low-voltage relay only after mastering the relay guide.
notes: This guide controls only an LED. Do not connect a household lamp directly to a breadboard.
validation: Compile-checked with Arduino AVR Boards 1.8.8 (UNO). Physical hardware and network operation have not been bench-tested; verify your exact modules.

title: Build an ultrasonic proximity indicator
introduction: The HC-SR04 sends a sound burst and reports the echo time. A desk-sized demonstration lights an LED and beeps when a target is closer than 20 cm.
purpose: Translate pulse timing into distance and learn to handle missing measurements.
learn: Measure echo duration with a timeout

parts.variant: Passive piezo module with signal input
Jumper set; select enough leads and correct connector types

extras: USB data cable and computer with Arduino IDE 2; cable must support data, not charging only.
Ruler and a flat, rigid target such as a book.

wiring.note: Only use a driven/low-current piezo module compatible with the GPIO signal.
Common ground for sensor and sound module.
10 µs trigger pulse.
Not safe directly into a 3.3 V ESP32 input.
tone() produces the audible frequency.
Separate LED output; not D9.
Keep the target perpendicular to the transducers.

steps: Connect HC-SR04 VCC/GND first, then TRIG to D9 and ECHO to D10.
Connect the passive piezo module signal to D3 and its supply pins as marked. Add the LED circuit on D6.
Upload for Arduino Uno and open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud.
Place a flat target at 10, 20 and 40 cm using a ruler. Compare the printed readings.
Remove or angle the target. A missing echo should print a clear message rather than reporting zero distance as an obstacle.
expected: Below 20 cm: LED on and short repeated tones.
Above 20 cm: LED off and no tone.
Invalid echo: output off and an explicit Serial Monitor message.
troubleshooting: Always no echo
Check TRIG/ECHO order, 5 V supply and common GND.
Noisy readings
Use a flat target, avoid soft fabric and wait between measurements.
No sound
An active buzzer is not the specified passive piezo module; confirm its input type.
extension: Add a middle warning band from 20–40 cm with a slower beep pattern using millis().
notes: This is a classroom proximity indicator, not a vehicle parking aid or collision-prevention system.
validation: Compile-checked with Arduino AVR Boards 1.8.8 (UNO). Physical hardware and network operation have not been bench-tested; verify your exact modules.

title: Build a temperature-controlled DC fan
introduction: A DHT22 measures room temperature. The controller energizes a relay above 30 °C and releases it below 28 °C, creating a small dead band that prevents relay chatter.
purpose: Demonstrate sensing, decision-making and switching a separate low-voltage load.

parts.role: Reverse-biased clamp across the small DC fan

parts.variant: Jumper set; select enough leads and correct connector types

extras: USB data cable and computer with Arduino IDE 2; cable must support data, not charging only.
5 V DC fan rated at no more than 0.3 A for this demonstration (not currently a catalog listing).
Regulated 5 V DC supply rated at least 1 A for fan and relay; size wiring and protection for the load.

wiring.note: For a bare 4-pin DHT22: front grille facing you, pin 1 VCC; pin 2 DATA; pin 3 NC; pin 4 GND.
Verify module labels if using a breakout.
Skip an extra resistor only if an appropriate pull-up is already present.
Do not join external +5 V to USB +5 V.
Power relay coil from the external supply; verify compatible 5 V IN input.
Example assumes active-low; verify before attaching the fan.
NC remains unused.
Small low-voltage DC fan only.
Diode is reverse biased in normal operation; never reverse it.
Separate logic power; only grounds are common.

steps: Disconnect all power. Identify relay VCC/GND/IN and COM/NO/NC; keep the fan disconnected initially.
Wire the DHT22 data and pull-up. Install DHT sensor library by Adafruit and Adafruit Unified Sensor through Library Manager.
Wire the relay control side. Set RELAY_ACTIVE_LOW to match the module; verify idle OFF and commanded ON with no load.
Wire the external 5 V supply, COM/NO contacts and fan. Add the reverse-biased diode across the fan, with its band toward fan positive.
Upload and watch temperature at 9600 baud. For a room-temperature test, temporarily set ON_C just above ambient and OFF_C two degrees lower.
Warm the sensor gently with your hand or nearby warm air, without liquids or a heat gun. Check turn-on/turn-off and disconnect the sensor data lead to observe the fault policy.
expected: At or above ON_C: fan on. At or below OFF_C: fan off. Between thresholds: retain state.
Invalid sensor reading: demonstration turns fan off and prints a fault.
troubleshooting: Relay runs backward
Correct RELAY_ACTIVE_LOW with the load disconnected.
DHT returns NaN
Check sensor type, pull-up, data pin and at least 2 s reading interval.
UNO resets when fan starts
Use an adequate separate supply, short wires and common ground; check diode polarity.
extension: Add a manual override button and a maximum runtime. For actual cooling, assess whether a sensor fault should force the fan ON instead.
notes: Low-voltage DC only. Do not wire mains AC to this student circuit.
Some relay modules need additional interface circuitry or idle bias to stay off during reset. Verify startup with the fan disconnected.
validation: Compile-checked with Arduino AVR Boards 1.8.8 (UNO). Physical hardware and network operation have not been bench-tested; verify your exact modules.

title: Build a hands-free model barrier
introduction: A small positional servo lifts a cardboard barrier when an object is near. The controller closes it only after the measured space stays clear for three seconds.
purpose: Combine sensing, timed logic and a mechanically moving output in a lightweight tabletop model.

parts.variant: Jumper set; select enough leads and correct connector types

extras: USB data cable and computer with Arduino IDE 2; cable must support data, not charging only.
Separate regulated 5 V supply rated at least 1 A for the small servo; verify stall demand.
Cardboard/paper arm, stable base, fasteners and tape.

wiring.note: Sensor is powered from the UNO, not the servo signal.
Only common ground joins the separate supplies.
D9 is not the servo signal in this guide.
Use UNO R3 with this direct connection.
Confirm wire colors from the actual servo.
Do not power the servo from an I/O pin or join external +5 V to USB +5 V.
UNO logic supply is independent.

steps: Select the 180° positional servo. The continuous-rotation version cannot hold a commanded angle.
Wire the HC-SR04 and servo signal, keeping servo power on its separate 5 V supply with common GND.
Install Servo by Arduino if it is not already available, and upload the sketch with the horn detached.
Check the 10° and 90° positions; adjust constants if needed without forcing mechanical end stops.
Attach a very light cardboard arm. Move a flat target within 15 cm: the arm opens. Move beyond 25 cm and keep it clear for 3 s: the arm closes.
Remove the echo/target and verify that invalid measurements command OPEN. Keep fingers out of the moving area.
expected: Starts open. Near target opens it. A clear reading beyond 25 cm for 3 s closes it.
No valid echo commands open. The 15–25 cm band holds the previous position and resets the clear timer.
troubleshooting: Servo spins continuously
You have a 360° continuous-rotation model; use the 180° version.
Servo jitters or board resets
Check separate supply capacity, common GND and mechanical load.
Never closes
The target must stay beyond 25 cm and within reliable sensor range for 3 s.
extension: Add a second sensor and an indicator LED. Explain why one ultrasonic sensor is insufficient for a real gate safety system.
notes: Tabletop model only: no full-size gate, heavy arm or moving machinery.
validation: Compile-checked with Arduino AVR Boards 1.8.8 (UNO). Physical hardware and network operation have not been bench-tested; verify your exact modules.

title: Build a GSM-based door-open notifier
introduction: A magnetic reed module reports a door or lid opening. An UNO sends AT commands to a SIM900A modem to request an SMS, then limits repeated messages.
purpose: Learn how a sensor event becomes a cellular message, including power, logic levels, registration and response handling.
learn: Check SIM readiness and network registration

parts.variant: SIM900A V4.0 kit — verify VCC5 and raw UART labels
Jumper set; select enough leads and correct connector types

extras: USB data cable and computer with Arduino IDE 2; cable must support data, not charging only.
Compatible antenna, active SIM with SMS credit/service, and verified 2G GSM 900/1800 coverage at the installation site.
Magnet and mounting hardware.
Separate regulated 5 V supply with at least 2 A transient capability for a kit documented to accept 5 V at VCC5; follow the kit manufacturer’s requirements.
TXU0202 UART level-translator breakout with both supply pins and OE exposed (not in current catalog).
Regulated 2.8 V logic supply for the translator low side, or an accessible verified modem VDD_EXT 2.8 V output within its current budget.

wiring.note: OE high enables translation; follow the breakout datasheet.
Use a verified 2.8 V rail, not the modem 5 V kit input.
5 V controller TX is translated to approximately 2.8 V.
2.8 V modem TX is translated up to 5 V.

wiring.to: Modem GND + translator GND + reed GND + all supply −
wiring.note: All UART signals require the same ground reference.
Verify CLOSED_LEVEL with magnet present before SMS testing.
Never connect +5 V to bare module VBAT or a VCC4 pin.
Place close to translator supply pin.
Second local decoupling capacitor.
Do not power the modem through the UNO 5 V pin.

steps: Confirm that your location and SIM support 2G GSM SMS. A newer SIM does not turn SIM900A into a 4G modem. Attach the compatible antenna before transmission.
Identify the kit power input and raw TTL UART pins using its documentation. If only RS232 or unidentified pins are exposed, stop and obtain the matching pinout; do not guess.

Wire the TXU0202 translator exactly as shown, with 5 V VCCA, 2.8 V VCCB, OE high, shared ground and both 100 nF capacitors. Do not substitute a bare divider for the modem-to-UNO receive level conversion.
Power the modem from its separate supply. Use its documented power-key/startup procedure; this sketch does not drive PWRKEY.
Verify the reed state with a meter or a small digitalRead test. Set CLOSED_LEVEL accordingly. Confirm the modem UART is configured for 9600 baud.
Replace PHONE with your own or a consenting recipient’s number in international format. Upload for Arduino Uno and open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud.
Allow startup and registration. Move the magnet away for at least one second; watch AT responses and the +CMGS acknowledgement. Close/reopen the contact and confirm the five-minute global cooldown.
expected: A stable open condition after startup triggers one SMS attempt.
Success is logged only after +CMGS; this acknowledges network/modem acceptance, not guaranteed handset delivery.
A persistent opening is not repeatedly messaged after success. Failed attempts wait at least five minutes before retrying.
troubleshooting: No AT reply
Check RX/TX crossover, shared GND, translator rails/OE, modem power state and 9600-baud setting.
Resets during SMS
Check voltage at the kit while transmitting, cable resistance and supply transient capacity.
Not registered
Check 2G service, antenna, SIM PIN/credit and AT+CREG? response.
No alert after changing code
PHONE must contain + followed by digits; placeholder X characters intentionally disable sending.
extension: Add a local status LED and a manually acknowledged event log. A later revision could use a locally supported LTE modem with the appropriate power and AT-command changes.
notes: The actual V4.0 kit schematic must be checked before wiring power or UART. The diagram explicitly uses an external translator for raw UART.
This teaching sketch blocks while waiting for AT responses and is not a certified security or emergency alarm. SMS attempts may incur carrier charges.
validation: Compile-checked with Arduino AVR Boards 1.8.8 (UNO). Physical hardware and network operation have not been bench-tested; verify your exact modules.

title: Build a local Wi-Fi room dashboard
introduction: An ESP32 reads temperature and humidity and serves a small dashboard to a phone connected directly to its Wi-Fi access point. No cloud account is needed.
purpose: Introduce embedded web interfaces while keeping the first networked project local and understandable.

parts.variant: Jumper set; select enough leads and correct connector types

extras: USB data cable and computer with Arduino IDE 2; cable must support data, not charging only.
Phone or laptop with Wi-Fi.

wiring.note: Power the sensor from 3.3 V for this guide.
Bare 4-pin sensor: pin 3 is not connected.
Use GPIO number, not a physical header position.
Never pull an ESP32 input to 5 V.
Use the development board USB input, not 5 V on 3V3.

steps: Verify that the board is the classic ESP32/ESP-WROOM-32 with GPIO27 exposed; this pin map is not for ESP32-C3/S3 boards.
Install esp32 by Espressif Systems in Boards Manager. Select ESP32 Dev Module and the correct port. Install the two Adafruit libraries listed below.
Wire the sensor to 3V3/GND/GPIO27 and add a 10 kΩ data pull-up to 3V3.
Replace AP_PASSWORD with a unique password of at least 8 characters. Upload, then open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud.
Join CircuitByte-Lab from your phone; accept staying connected when the phone reports no Internet. Open the local HTTP address printed by Serial Monitor, usually 192.168.4.1.
Watch readings refresh every 3 s. Disconnect sensor data to verify the unavailable message, then reconnect and allow the next sample.
expected: The ESP32 creates its own password-protected Wi-Fi network.
The page displays temperature, humidity and sample age; invalid samples display --.
Readings remain local to the device. This sketch does not upload history to CircuitByte or the cloud.
troubleshooting: Cannot find Wi-Fi
Confirm the upload completed, check power and read Serial Monitor for AP errors.
Page cannot load
Stay on the ESP32 Wi-Fi and use http:// with the printed IP, not https://. Disable automatic switching to mobile data if needed.
Sensor unavailable
Check GPIO27, 3.3 V supply, pull-up, sensor type and wiring length.
extension: Add minimum/maximum readings and a small history buffer. Explain what is lost when power is removed and how microSD logging could preserve it.
notes: Do not connect 5 V logic to ESP32 GPIO. The dashboard is a local HTTP teaching example; do not expose it directly to the public Internet.
validation: Compile-checked with Espressif ESP32 core 3.3.0. Physical hardware and network operation have not been bench-tested; verify your exact modules.

title: Build a three-LED scanning light
introduction: Three small LEDs light one after another and reverse direction like a miniature scanning light. This project joins low-voltage wiring, arrays, for loops and reusable functions in one visible result.
purpose: Practice basic Arduino programming by building a repeatable three-light scanning pattern with common catalog components.
learn: Wire three LEDs with separate current-limiting resistors
Use an array to store three output pins
Read a for loop that moves the light forward and backward
Change a function parameter to control animation speed

parts.variant: Three 5 mm indicator LEDs (same color recommended)
Three separate 330 Ω, ¼ W resistors
Enough male-to-male jumpers for three outputs and common GND

extras: A computer with Arduino IDE 2 installed and an appropriate USB data cable.
A phone camera (optional) to record and compare animation speeds.

wiring.note: LED 1 cathode (−) to common GND.
LED 2 cathode (−) to common GND.
LED 3 cathode (−) to common GND.
Verify rail continuity; some breadboard rails are split.
Unplug before moving jumper wires.

steps: Disconnect the UNO from USB. Insert three LEDs on separate breadboard rows; do not place both legs of one LED in the same connected row.
Connect D8, D9 and D10 individually to an LED anode through one 330 Ω resistor per LED.
Connect each LED cathode to a verified common GND rail, then connect the rail to UNO GND.
Follow the schematic and the pin-by-pin wiring map, then compare every connection before applying power.
Connect the board, select Arduino Uno and the right port in Arduino IDE, and upload three-led-scanner.ino.
Observe the order 1 → 2 → 3 → 2, repeating. Change stepDelayMs from 170 to 350 and re-upload to slow the effect.
expected: Exactly one LED is illuminated at a time.
The pattern travels from LED 1 to LED 3 and back through LED 2, repeating.
Increasing stepDelayMs makes the pattern visibly slower.
troubleshooting: No LEDs illuminate
Check the selected board/port, uploaded sketch, D8–D10 connections, common ground and LED polarity.
One LED stays dark
Disconnect power and check that LED's resistor, polarity, output pin and breadboard row.
All three stay on
Confirm each output drives only one resistor/LED branch; check for breadboard row shorts and try the upload again.
Pattern seems irregular
Verify the array order {8, 9, 10} and that each LED matches its intended digital pin.
UNO resets or USB disconnects
Unplug immediately and inspect for a short between supply and GND.
extension: Add a fourth LED and resistor on D11 and extend ledPins. Predict the new forward/reverse behavior before uploading.
flow: Turn on LED at current array index
notes: Keep USB unplugged during assembly and troubleshooting. This is a 5 V logic project, not a mains lighting controller.
Use a separate resistor for every LED; do not put several LEDs in parallel behind one resistor.
UNO output pins must not directly power motors, relays or other high-current loads.
Confirm the actual breadboard's rail and strip continuity; two holes in the same strip are electrically joined.
libraries: Arduino AVR Boards core; no external libraries required
validation: Source reviewed for Arduino UNO logic and array bounds. Hardware operation and Arduino IDE compilation have not been independently bench-verified.

title: Build a joystick-controlled four-way light
introduction: A two-axis joystick contains two potentiometers. Your Arduino reads their analog values and lights one of four LEDs depending on which direction you move the stick.
purpose: Learn to translate two analog inputs into decisions and physical outputs using common CircuitByte components.
learn: Read X and Y using analogRead()
Use if/else conditions and an adjustable dead zone

parts.role: Reads joystick and drives indicator LEDs

parts.variant: Two-axis analog joystick module with VRx, VRy, VCC, GND pins

parts.role: Shows up, down, left and right

parts.variant: Four 330 Ω ¼ W resistors, one per LED
parts.role: Keeps each LED current within a safe range

parts.variant: Jumper wires with suitable male/female ends

extras: Computer, Arduino IDE 2 and USB data cable.
Paper labels for LEFT, RIGHT, UP and DOWN LEDs (optional).

wiring.note: Only if the joystick board is rated for 5 V operation.
Match printed labels on the physical module.
Analog horizontal axis; reverse interpretations if needed.
Analog vertical axis.

wiring.to: LEFT LED anode (+); cathode to GND
wiring.note: Use a separate resistor for this LED.

wiring.to: RIGHT LED anode (+); cathode to GND
wiring.note: Use a separate resistor for this LED.

wiring.to: UP LED anode (+); cathode to GND
wiring.note: Use a separate resistor for this LED.

wiring.to: DOWN LED anode (+); cathode to GND
wiring.note: Use a separate resistor for this LED.

steps: Unplug UNO USB and identify the joystick module pin labels.
Connect VCC/GND/VRx/VRy to the corresponding UNO pins in the table; do not swap supply with a signal pin.
Add four separate LED-resistor branches to D5, D6, D9 and D10 and connect their cathodes to GND.
Upload the original sketch with the correct board and port selected.
Open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud to read X and Y values. Verify the resting readings are near midpoint.
Tilt the joystick one direction at a time; one matching LED should light. To reverse a direction, change which pin or comparison is assigned.
If the stick causes an LED to flicker at rest, increase the deadZone constant and re-upload.
expected: All four LEDs are off when the stick remains near its center position.
Moving left or right lights the corresponding single horizontal LED.
Moving up or down lights the corresponding single vertical LED.
Diagonal motion can light one horizontal and one vertical LED concurrently.
troubleshooting: All LEDs stay off
Check joystick VCC/GND, VRx/VRy, serial ADC readings, resistors and LED polarity.
Direction reversed
Joystick orientation varies. Swap axis comparison or swap the labels of LEDs.
Light flickers at center
Increase the deadZone, inspect the idle analog readings and improve ground connections.
UNO gets hot or disconnects
Unplug immediately and inspect shorts between 5V and GND.
extension: Use the joystick SW button (if fitted) on D2 with INPUT_PULLUP to toggle whether direction indicators are enabled.
flow: Compare each axis with center and dead zone
Show current values on Serial Monitor
notes: The joystick module may face a different direction or have reversed axis polarity; calibrate using Serial Monitor.
Check exact module voltage and pin labels before wiring. Joystick SW is intentionally unused in the basic build.
Every bare LED needs its own resistor; no external motor or mains load is controlled by this sketch.
libraries: No external libraries. Standard Arduino core functions only.
validation: Original educational design: software and wiring have undergone a source-level review; hardware has not been bench-tested.

title: Build a temperature and humidity LCD monitor
introduction: An Arduino reads a DHT22 sensor and displays room temperature and relative humidity on a two-line I²C LCD. The project combines sensor timing, external libraries, display communication and invalid-reading handling.
purpose: Create a stand-alone environmental display using listed CircuitByte components, without Wi-Fi, cloud accounts or internet connectivity.
learn: Use the I²C bus at A4/A5 on an UNO
Install and call documented sensor and LCD libraries
Detect failed sensor reads instead of displaying misleading values

parts.role: Controller for the sensor and display

parts.variant: DHT22/AM2302 temperature and humidity sensor, pinout verified
16 × 2 character LCD with PCF8574/MCP23008-compatible I²C backpack
10 kΩ ¼ W resistor for a bare DHT22 (omit if the breakout has a verified pull-up)
parts.role: Pulls DHT data line up to sensor VCC
Supports the optional pull-up and wire junctions

parts.variant: Jumper wires suited to module connectors

extras: Computer, USB data cable and Arduino IDE 2.
Install 'DHT sensor library' by Adafruit and 'Adafruit Unified Sensor' in Library Manager.
Install 'hd44780' by Bill Perry in Library Manager; use its I2Cexp interface.
Optionally run the separate I²C scanner lesson first to troubleshoot module communication.

wiring.note: For a verified 5 V I²C LCD backpack only.
Share ground between peripherals.
UNO I²C data.
UNO I²C clock.
Bare DHT22 pin 1 at the specified orientation; module pin order may differ.
On bare DHT22, signal is pin 2; pin 3 is not connected.
Do not add redundant pull-ups when the module already provides one.

steps: Disconnect USB and inspect the exact DHT22 sensor packaging and the LCD backpack pin labels.
Wire SDA to A4, SCL to A5, and connect verified-compatible power/ground to the I²C LCD.
Connect the DHT22 sensor to pin D2 and add the 10 kΩ data pull-up only if the board does not include one.
Install the Adafruit DHT sensor library, Unified Sensor dependency and Bill Perry hd44780 library using Arduino Library Manager.
Upload the example and observe the LCD. It should show temperature on row 1 and humidity on row 2.
Breathe near (but not onto or into) the sensor and observe the humidity change after a few refreshes.
Disconnect the sensor DATA wire with power off to test that the display reports unavailable readings.
expected: The LCD shows a temperature reading in Celsius and relative humidity in percent.
Readings refresh every 2.5 seconds.
If the sensor cannot be read, the LCD shows a Sensor error indication instead of a stale number.
troubleshooting: LCD lights but shows blocks
Check contrast adjustment and I²C wiring; run the library's I2CexpDiag diagnostic.
LCD not detected
Check A4/A5 wiring, common ground and the backpack's correct operating voltage.
Sensor error
Confirm DHT22 vs DHT11, D2 DATA, pull-up, power and the sensor's pin order.
Library missing at compile time
Install the named libraries and check which header file the compiler says is missing.
extension: Create a comfort indicator with an LED that turns on if the measured temperature exceeds a user-selected threshold. This is educational monitoring, not an alarm system.
notes: This project is an environmental demonstration, not a calibrated measurement or safety device.
The LCD requires a compatible I²C backpack; hd44780_I2Cexp detects many PCF8574/MCP23008 backpacks automatically but not every possible module.
Do not connect 5 V I²C lines to a 3.3 V-only controller. The specified board here is UNO 5 V.
A bare four-pin DHT22 and a preassembled three-pin module have different pinouts; verify the physical component.
libraries: DHT sensor library by Adafruit (install the Unified Sensor dependency)
validation: Code written against documented Adafruit DHT and hd44780 interfaces; no physical bench test performed. Confirm actual LCD backpack and DHT22 module variants before wiring.

title: Build a microSD light-level data logger
introduction: Instead of simply displaying sensor values, log them to a CSV file on a microSD card. The UNO samples an analog light sensor at a fixed interval and saves readings for later graphing.
purpose: Practice analog acquisition, SPI storage, CSV files, non-blocking interval checks and recoverable storage errors.
learn: Read the analog voltage of a light-sensor module
Save a timestamped CSV on a microSD card
Understand why the adapter's 3.3 V signal levels must be checked

parts.variant: Light-dependent resistor sensor module with an analog AO output
SPI microSD module; MUST confirm onboard regulation and 5 V input logic compatibility or add a suitable level shifter
Jumper wires suited to actual module headers

extras: A compatible microSD card formatted FAT16/FAT32 as supported by the Arduino SD library; prepare it on a computer.
A separate bidirectional/unidirectional 5 V-to-3.3 V SPI logic-level adapter when required by the exact microSD breakout. Do not bypass this check.
Computer, Arduino IDE 2, appropriate USB data cable and a microSD card reader.
Use the Arduino SD and SPI libraries supplied with the board environment; no network connection is needed.

wiring.note: Confirm the exact AO module supply rating.

wiring.to: Light sensor GND and SD module GND
wiring.note: Both devices share the UNO reference.
Use AO, not DO, so the logger records a continuously varying ADC value.
5 V UNO output requires level translation unless breakout explicitly supports 5 V logic.
Keep UNO 5 V signal off 3.3 V-only SD pins.
3.3 V output from the SD usually meets UNO digital-high threshold; verify circuit.
SPI clock must respect the actual module logic rating.
Use 5 V only if the breakout has a suitable regulator. Otherwise follow its 3.3 V supply specification.

steps: Confirm whether the SD breakout includes both a voltage regulator and logic-level translation. If not, use a suitable level shifter; do not connect 5 V UNO outputs directly to SD card pins.
With USB disconnected, wire the analog light-sensor output to A0 and confirm a common GND.
Wire the SPI pins CS D10, MOSI D11, MISO D12 and SCK D13 through the proper logic-compatible interface.
Format a compatible card FAT16/FAT32, insert it with power off, then upload the original logger sketch.
Open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud and verify that it reports successful SD initialization and appends a row every five seconds.
Cover and uncover the sensor; verify that ADC values change in Serial Monitor and in LIGHT.CSV.
Disconnect power normally, remove the card, and inspect the CSV in a spreadsheet. Compare light changes against the recorded millis timestamps.
expected: The file LIGHT.CSV is created with a header if it does not already exist.
Every five seconds, a new CSV row records milliseconds since boot and an ADC reading from 0 to 1023.
Covering/uncovering the LDR changes the reading; the direction depends on sensor circuit design.
If SD cannot initialize, the logger reports an error on Serial Monitor rather than silently claiming data was saved.
troubleshooting: SD.begin failed
Check filesystem, card, CS pin D10, MISO/MOSI/SCK wiring, stable power and logic-level compatibility.
No CSV appears
Confirm SD initialization succeeded, a compatible FAT filesystem is used and the sketch has permission to create files.
Always 0 or 1023
Check AO vs DO on the sensor and confirm the sensor operates within 0–5 V at the UNO analog input.
Unchanging readings
Check the sensor's analog output and cover/uncover its LDR; confirm supply and ground.
Unexpected resets
Stop and inspect power instability, shorts and the breakout's regulator/current demand.
extension: Replace millis-based time with a DS3231 clock. Record a real calendar timestamp after verifying RTC module battery/charging safety and creating a suitable RTC initialization routine.
notes: WARNING: An SD module's 3.3 V regulator is not evidence its SPI inputs tolerate 5 V. Use a 5 V-compatible breakout with true level shifting or add a compatible translator.
Never hot-plug a microSD card while the sketch is writing; unmount by powering down before removal.
This project measures relative light level, not calibrated lux. Date/time is uptime since power-on, not a real clock.
SD cards and adapters are subject to write failure; verify exported CSV before relying on collected measurements.
libraries: SD library (Arduino Library Manager / standard Arduino library)
validation: Source-level review only. The exact microSD module and optional level shifter have not been inspected or bench-tested; hardware-compatibility verification is mandatory.
